**Verdict:** Yes. Hormozi would have you name the real weaknesses your buyers already see, claim them before they raise them, and put the benefit after "but." He says "nothing more powerful than damaging admissions" ([[yt-JDR-R--4HhM]] @ 12:30).

**Based on:** said it (confidence: high). Hormozi makes this point several times in [14 Years of Marketing Advice in 35 Minutes](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM), and the vault has a dedicated page, [[marketing/copywriting/damaging-admissions]].

**Why they'd say it**
- Trust beats promise: "what you'll sacrifice in promise you'll gain in trust and trust trumps promise" ([[yt-JDR-R--4HhM]] @ 13:09, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=789s)
- The buyer already has the objection: "the prospect is already thinking them but if you can claim them instead of them thinking them you acknowledge them gain trust" (@ 15:39)
- Plain claims don't persuade: "anyone can say that but what people won't say is the truth" (@ 16:15)

**How to word it**

The shape is *flaw, flaw, but the claim you want believed*. Whatever follows "but" is what the reader takes away, so put the flaw first and the claim last. He makes the point with a pair of examples: "these markers write four times longer but they smell like crap" puts the smell in the foreground, and "they smell like crap but they write four times longer" puts the writing in the foreground (@ 14:26).

His own examples follow that shape:
- "our websites are ugly as hell but they convert" (@ 15:03)
- "our gym has honestly pretty terrible parking our AC is kind of on and off i don't have the best equipment but our sessions are more fun than everyone else's cuz it's all we've got" (@ 15:39)

Steps:
1. Write down every complaint, objection and bad review you know of. He says to do exactly this (@ 15:03).
2. Keep the flaws you can answer after "but" with something true and checkable. "Proof will always outdo promise" (@ 3:44).
3. Write each one as flaw, then "but", then the claim.
4. Humor is a bonus, not a requirement: "if you can do with humor you get even more bonus points" (@ 15:39). It's the first thing he'd cut if he had to cut something (@ 33:58).

Pair this with "always call out who you're looking for and bonus points who you're not looking for" (@ 5:02, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=302s). The people a flaw would put off can then opt out before they click.

**What would change their answer**
- If buyers don't already think of the flaw, the reason he gives for raising it no longer applies. This is my extrapolation from his rule.
- If you can't back up the "but" with proof, the admission just reads as weakness. This follows from "proof will always outdo promise."
- If the flaw stops people from buying, fix the offer first: "if we can't get enough people to say yes we need to make the offer better" ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]] @ 1:25:23).

**One caveat that's mine, not Hormozi's:** the research he cites on admitting bias is unnamed, and the Eminem story is an illustration rather than data. Test an admission ad against your current one instead of assuming it wins. That fits his own rule of letting the market and tests decide ([[thinking/hormozi]]).

**Verdict:** Hormozi calls 80% monthly retention (about 20% monthly churn) typical for a paid online community. Under 10% churn is best, and 30% or more churn is "not good." Worry when more than 30% of members leave in a month, or when cancels outrun joins. If your average is in the typical range, he'd say to look at when people leave, not at the average.

**Based on:** said it. The numbers and thresholds are his, from one video. The cohort check in the last bullet below is my application of his cohort figures, not his wording.

**Why they'd say it**
- The benchmark: "the platform average across School is 80% monthly retention. So said differently, it's 20% churn." "the best groups have less than 10% churn" and "The not good groups have less than 70% retention, aka 30% or higher." ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 1:39, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=99s. The auto-captions spell the platform "School"; it's Skool.)
- The alarm threshold: "if less than seven out of 10 people want to stay on a monthly basis, you probably need to work on your retention more than anything else. It'll be the highest ROI lever." ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 1:39)
- Growth test: track "joins versus cancels, and then force yourself to label the businesses growing, flat, or declining based on that." ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 0:33)
- Why small churn changes matter: "you didn't just get a 10 or 12% boost, you got a double in the LTV per customer." ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 2:13)
- Don't panic about early churn: "month one to three are the highest churn," at "20% plus during these months" ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 3:19–3:53). "don't overhaul your entire business because your month one churn sucks," "unless basically everyone's leaving, in which case, yes, you should go fix that." ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 4:24–4:57)
- Young groups look worse: "if your community or recurring revenue thing is less than 90 days old, then your churn is always going to be inflated." ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 4:24)
- Cohort targets: past day 90 "it drops to around 10% or less," and "by month six… it goes from like 10% to 2%." ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 3:53)
- My inference from those cohort figures, not his words: if members past day 90 still churn near the blended 20%, you haven't reached the cliff yet.

**What they've done:** After many cancellations citing price, Skool added a $9 tier under its $99 one ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 7:40). For cancellations, he says to "for every 20 cancels or so, review the top one or two reasons, and then fix those" ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 6:35). He also says "annual always has lower churn than monthly" ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 15:52).

**What would change their answer**
- He scopes the benchmark himself: "this isn't uh churn for like an insurance premium or an alarm system." It's for online, consumer, or remote services, so a high-ticket or B2B community may not fit.
- Cohort age matters. A group with mostly new members will look worse than it is.
- Annual billing churns less, so don't compare an annual community to monthly benchmarks.
- Source depth: all 14 churn statements in the vault come from one video (2026-03-24, "How to Get Your Customers to Stay FOREVER"). The figures are Skool platform averages that he credits to Skool's founder, Sam, and Skool is a platform he's involved with. Treat them as one operator's platform data, not an independent benchmark.

My own note, not from the vault: one platform-wide average mixes healthy and struggling groups, so use 80% as a sanity check, not a target.

I can file this as `derived/` if you want to keep it.

**Verdict:** Pay it off. Hormozi would clear the $60k from profit over a few months, ahead of new growth spending, rather than emptying the cash you'd use to grow. He gave this call to a profitable service business with about $60k of debt, and his reason is that debt adds risk that "tends to come due" over time.

**Based on:** said it. The situation matches yours, but the vault has only one consult on it.

**Why they'd say it**
- Debt risk: "debt increases risk. Risk when multiplied over a long time horizon tends to come due." ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 9:10; https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=550s)
- He's skeptical of borrowing to grow: "why did I take the, you know, the debt out to begin with? A lot of times it's like cuz I wanted to grow faster." (same, @ 9:10)
- His lean: "I tend to skew like very close to the Ramsey side" (same, @ 8:37). He also says "I'd say this is more of an emotional thing, but it's just this back of mind thing" (same, @ 8:37).
- The plan he endorsed: the owner was "allocating about 10% of our profit going towards paying off some of our debt" (same, @ 0:33), aiming to "pay off completely in the next four to five months." Hormozi replied "Okay, good." (same, @ 8:37). In the priority list, the payoff was second, after a price raise and before the funnel and ad fixes: "Two is you're going to continue to pay off the debt." (same, @ 30:45)
- On the growth side, the test is a return you can measure, not whether you have cash: "if you know that's where the money's coming from, by all means, spend more." (same, @ 11:21)
- Applied to your case (my extrapolation, not his words about debt): "You cannot take any risk on if you have no time and no money." ([[yt-jfW6gL6hKhk]] @ 13:04; https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=784s). That argues against paying the whole $60k out of the cash that funds growth in one go.

**What they've done:** The owner planned to pay the debt from profit over four to five months. The one-year follow-up (same source, @ 34:31) says sales were on track for $2.3–2.5M, up from about $1.25M, but it never mentions the debt. We don't know whether it was cleared on schedule.

**What would change their answer**
- A growth channel with a return you can measure (stable CAC and ROAS, attribution checked). Then he'd keep spending: "we just want to continue to spend month over month provided our ROAS and our CAC stay more or less the same." (same, @ 10:48). Even so, for that owner the order was fix the funnel and ads first, then raise spend, with the debt payoff ranked above the spend increase. He doesn't say how to split the two.
- The interest rate. The vault never discusses it. If your rate is low and you can prove a return above it, keeping the cash is the better math. This is beyond what he addressed (not in the vault).

**Caveats:** Finance isn't one of the areas where the profile lists him as credible. Those are offers, sales, ads, licensing and retention. This is one consult, and the argument is mostly the risk line above. He also takes a different view in June 2026, when he treats heavy debt in a fund example as how a fund manager gets rich. The tensions page notes the scopes differ, since that's fund management rather than an operating business ([[tensions]]).

**My own point, not his:** The rate matters more than he lets on, and he never mentions it. If your debt is cheap and your growth returns are proven, keeping the cash is the stronger case.

**Verdict:** No. Raise prices about 10% and treat it as a test. Keep the raise while your close rate stays above roughly 65%. Holding prices to protect the close rate is the mistake he'd call out. An 82% close rate tells him you're underpriced.

**Based on:** said it. He addressed nearly this exact business on camera: an HVAC duct-cleaning company at about $1.25M a year, 38% net margin and an 82% close rate ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]], May 2026). Applying it to your company is an inference, but the advice is his.

**Why they'd say it**
- Price raises can increase trust: "if you raise your prices, what sometimes happens is that the conviction of the customer that you can actually deliver on the promise you're making goes up." ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 7:00, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=420s)
- On the close rate: "So whenever I hear 80% or over 80% close rates, I usually know that there's room in sale." (@ 8:06, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=486s)
- On the fear: "they're so afraid of charging money that they actually sell themselves out of a sale" (@ 7:33, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=453s)
- On the line to watch: "As long as we close more than 65%, we make more money." (@ 8:06)

**What they've done:** At the same company, he had the owner raise prices 23% after an earlier workshop, then proposed a further 10%. He penciled that as roughly a 25% rise in net profit at last year's volume and called it "more asking than telling," meaning a test.

**The math for your business (my arithmetic, not his)**
- A 10% raise at the same volume adds about $120K a year, nearly all of it profit: roughly $456K to $576K, about +26%.
- Break-even close rate = 82% × (margin per job today) ÷ (margin per job after the raise). If every cost moves with each closed job, that gives 82 × 38 ÷ 48 ≈ 65%, his number. Fixed overhead such as office, trucks or salaried staff pushes the break-even higher, so use your own cost split before relying on 65%.

**Discount these parts**
- The "closed more" result after the 23% raise is Hormozi's account. On camera the owner only says "Right."
- The one-year follow-up is the owner's own report that he's on track for $2.3–2.5M. It doesn't report close rate, so it doesn't show the raise held conversion.
- The video is also a funnel. It pitches his free roadmap and booking calls, and the vault flags his self-interest ([[profile]]). The pricing point doesn't depend on buying anything, but weigh his numbers accordingly.

**What would change their answer:** If the close rate falls below your break-even after the raise, he'd back off. That line is 65% for a 10% raise. My inference breaks if most of your 82% comes from a segment that wouldn't respond to a higher price the way his clients did. Check close rate by lead source before you raise.

Related: [[pricing/premium-pricing/raising-prices-to-close-more]], [[thinking/hormozi]]. If you want to keep this, I can file it to `derived/`.

**Verdict:** Hormozi tells this as a "same work, more zeros" story. Banks told him the same business would be worth about four times more on the NASDAQ than where it had listed. That pushed him toward IPO marketing, and his first big payoff was roughly $7–8 million in equity for about nine months of work with a company before its IPO.

**Based on:** said it (Diary of a CEO, E235, 3 April 2023, Hormozi speaking). Source: [[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo. Confidence is high on what he said. The dollar figures are his recollection and he hedges them.

**The story, in order**

1. His company had listed on a European exchange. Later, on a roadshow with about 20 investment banks for a possible IPO in another country, the banks told him that "the exact same business would be worth four times more" on the NASDAQ. He says that meant his net worth would rise by the same multiple just from moving the business to a different exchange. ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]] @ 1:34:12)
2. A couple of years later he asked where his skills were in demand. He says he "looked for an industry where my skill set was in least Supply but highest demand" and found it in social media marketing and storytelling for companies about to IPO. "If you have a good story it can swing your valuation by hundreds of millions." ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]] @ 1:34:43 and 1:35:17)
3. The equity deal: he worked with a company before its IPO, which he says listed at "3 billion" in value. He took equity as part of the pay for nine to twelve months of work, which he calls "basically freelance." On IPO day he estimates that equity was worth roughly $7–8 million. He contrasts this with the roughly $1,000 a local gym would have paid for the same skills. He hedges the value because the share price moved. ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]] @ 1:35:17 to 1:35:51)
4. He later started a company (the captions read "flight story") that began in the IPO market and then moved into biotech. ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]] @ 1:36:23)

**Lesson he draws:** Capital markets change what the same work is worth. In his leverage list he puts public money at the top of capital: "there's just significantly more capital in that" ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]] @ 1:45:47), then "same work more zeros" ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]] @ 1:46:20).

**Caveats on the premise**
- The 4x is a banker's pitch as he recounts it, and he moves the business to NASDAQ only hypothetically. He doesn't say the company moved, or what value it realized.
- The equity deal wasn't his own company's IPO. It was equity in a different company he was working for before that company's IPO.
- The auto-captions garble the sentence about his net worth ("would be Forex"). I've paraphrased it rather than quoting it.

**Vault gap:** The source is marked `compiled` in `sources.yaml`, but no wiki page mentions the NASDAQ or the IPO deal. Only `raw/` has it. I searched the files directly with Grep rather than the `wwxd` CLI, since the CLI call needed approval. I can add this story to the wiki with citations, or save this answer to `derived/` if you want to keep it.

**Verdict:** The premise is off. Hormozi didn't tell that roofer to stop door-knocking. He told him to go all in on door-to-door as his primary growth engine, and the vault has no advice to move the budget into Google Ads for this owner.

He said it to Caleb, owner of Keys Roofing in St. Louis, a two-month-old company doing about $20K a month from door-knocking and referrals. The consult is the August 2026 "Scale or Fail" episode.

**Based on:** said it (high confidence)

**Why they'd say it**
- The owner was already good at door-knocking. Hormozi: "It's what you're good at." ([[yt-o64cI6tebnU]] @ 10:21, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=621s)
- Hormozi's stated rule for limited time and money: "I want to focus all efforts on the highest return stuff that you can do right now." ([[yt-o64cI6tebnU]] @ 3:16, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=196s)
- For scale, he said: "Now I think that in terms of scale, you should go all in door to door." ([[yt-o64cI6tebnU]] @ 9:49, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=589s)
- He framed the rep commission per door: "So, it's like how much money do you want to make? Just knock that many doors." ([[yt-o64cI6tebnU]] @ 10:54, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=654s)
- Later, he restated the plan: "the first thing we said was go all in on door to door as primary growth engine." ([[yt-o64cI6tebnU]] @ 24:27, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=1467s)

His general rule is to fix what already works before adding a channel, which fits this case. See [[thinking/hormozi]] ("Fixes what already exists, cheapest first").

**What they've done:** In the 90-day follow-up, the guest reported revenue going from under $32K to about $247K. The unit isn't stated, and these are the guest's own numbers.

**Where the Google Ads idea might come from:** The closest match is a different consult, a 2026 HVAC-duct cleaning business (ProShine, [[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]]). There he ranked ad fixes and raising ad spend ahead of outbound to HOAs, and suggested bidding on the client's own brand name. That business didn't drop a working channel for ads.

**What would change their answer:** Door-knocking stopped converting, for example if the cost per signed job rose above what each job pays. His rules would then say to test another channel. He would only scale paid ads once returns are proven, though: "we just want to continue to spend month over month provided our ROAS and our CAC stay more or less the same." ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 10:48, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=648s)
